      HOW TO WRITE TO OUTLET
      ----------------------
Letters are accepted  in  almost
any form for publication in our
OUTLETTERS: BASIC PRINT or  DATA
statements, handwritten or typed
pages, a simple  JOTTER  program
is provided in Issue 2(Disk #4);
mailbox messages via Prestel No.
014703943 but the easiest for us
to edit are Tasword 2 files with
the right-hand margin set at 32.

Please state if there should  be
parts of your letter you do  not
wish published but we always use
our discretion  anyway.  Letters
may also be edited  for  clarity
and length... Please ask if  you
welcome  direct   correspondence
from other OUTLET readers and we
will publish your full address.

From: Alistair McColl, CLYDEBANK

Dear Brian & Ron,

I would like some help to amend
CAL-PLAN in Issue No.16 to print
out on A4 paper. My set-up is
Disciple Interface & Mannesmann
Tally MT80 printer.

CAL-PLAN already gives A4 print-
outs on the Disciple and should
work o.k. on your system without
change.The printer options don't
appear until AFTER the calendar
has been calculated following
input of the year when a prompt
asks "screen or printer?". I'm
sure you will find this works
but if not, write again saying
exactly what occurs. - Brian

from E.M.Duffield,  CRAWLEY

Dear Ron & Brian,

I cannot return Issue 20 because
I dropped a glass of water on
it. Believe it or not, after
thoroughly drying out the disc
it worked fairly well. After
running a couple of times even
the BAD Sectors Loaded.

The second part of Brian's reply
to Mr D. P. Smart Issue 20 is
the short answer. I understood
"PATCH" to mean moving a certain
number of machine code
instructions to a place in RAM
where they can be corrected and
run. There are some, ifs and
buts, to consider, however I'm

very thankful for the inquiry,
and if Mr Smart is still unable
to understand, perhaps he could
rephrase his question.

It may be of interest to other
readers that I purchased a 5.25"
double-sided 780K drive for
`39.10. These are brand new,inc.
postage and VAT. They work on my
MGT PLUS D and QL but not on the
Atari ST - probably because they
are the old-fashioned 4" deep
style. Telephone: 0223 327602

A further developement in disc
washing, is it cured a disc that
refused to fully format on any
of three Computers or three
drives. I cracked open the case
on three sides (not the metal
window side).

On testing the 3 Discs you sent
I find that Issue 16 is also
faulty at the same sector 38:8.
It seems unlikely both discs
should be faulty at the same
spot. My QL Disc Doctor type of
program can read sector 38:8
alright but my printer is not
quite compatible with the pro-
gram.I enclose the first version
of 16 & 20 in case your Plus D
expert wishes to investigate.

I noticed the word "PATCH" used
in connection with Viruses. I
don't know what it all meant,
but my previous comments still
hold good.     - E.M. Duffield

Many thanks. We'll investigate
the disc error.         - Brian

To Ray Floyd from Brian

We cannot at the moment supply a
+3 disc version of OUTLET but we
are definitely considering doing
so if we can raise the cash to
buy a +3 and a second drive with
which to duplicate each issue.

Can any other reader help with
the printer problem as I don't
have either the +3 or the Tandy
printer? In passing I would
suggest that anyone with any
problems like this give more
details of what they have tried.

For example, has the printer got
a self-test mode and have you
tried it? Have you had the
printer working at all on ANY

system? Have you tried to LPRINT
from BASIC or merely tried to
print something out from an
application such as a word-
processor or a graphics program?
Does your +3 manual say anything
about initializing the printer
interface, e.g. with FORMAT "P"
or suchlike and if so have you
tried it? Sorry if these sound
like trivial have-you-plugged-
the printer-in-the-mains-type
questions but, who knows?! The
more information given - the
more chance of assistance.

Again, with the Opus problem,you
say "nothing happens" when you
type "run". Do you get an OK
message or an error message (if
so, what?) or does the computer

keyboard "lock up" preventing
further entry? How many times
did you try? Are you CERTAIN
there was a disc in the drive?If
not, try again but if you know
you had a disc in the drive then
try thoroughly cleaning the edge
connector of the Spectrum with a
soft rubber eraser and try again
(also check the interfaces are
rammed together firmly!).

None of the above is meant to be
insulting - it's just an
impersonal, mechanical method of
problem-solving by first
eliminating the obvious and
gathering as much information as
possible!

Meanwhile, can anyone else offer
any help? - Brian

From: Alistair Thomas, INVERESK

I have a couple of technical
questions. Firstly, "That's the
Ticket!" - I enjoyed this a lot
and the graphics were especially
interesting. this was because of
the multi-coloured borders which
enhanced their graphics a great
deal. In particular, the picture
of the sunrise and silhouetted
mountain struck me as being one
of the most impressve graphics
I've ever seen on the Spectrum.
This is an effect I'd like to
use myself.Have you ever printed
the method? I know there was
something about manipulating the
border in one OUTCLASS (#15?)
but I don't remember it being
the same thing.

The other question is about
"AUTOCHARS". I believe this
creates a new character set by
"smearing" the standard set one
pixel to the right.I understand,
however, this is only done once
and the new set is then stored
in memory. I'm interested in
using the technique in an adven-
ture I'm writing and, as memory
space is paramount,was wondering
if it would be practical to
smear each character as it is
printed, i.e. could text be
stored in terms of references to
the standard Sinclair set and
smeared only when needed on
screen as opposed to being
stored in memory? Would this be
too slow or invalid for some
other reason?

If it were possible, do you know
how long the calculation would
take per character?

Yours,

Alistair G. Thomas

To Alistair Thomas from Brian

To take your last question first
I must say it's a fascinating
idea and I think it would work!
I have added this to my project
list and will see what I can do.
If it works out I'll put it in a
future issue. Meanwhile you may
care to read AUTOINFO in Issue 7
which describes exactly how
AUTOCHARS works in great detail
and also OUTCLASS in Issue 5 for
tips on saving memory.

Now, the border graphics effect
is created thus:

10 PAUSE 1 : BORDER 6 : BORDER 4
: BORDER 5 : BORDER 0: BORDER 2:
BORDER 7 : GO TO 10

I think it works because the
PAUSE 1 delays the video signal
by one fiftieth of a second
which exactly matches the time
it takes for the BORDER command
to fully change. You can also
experiment with the PAUSE 1 at
the end of the BORDER commands
rather than at the front. To get
thicker stripes you just repeat,
e.g.

10 PAUSE 1: BORDER 5: BORDER 5:
BORDER 5: BORDER 5: BORDER 5:
BORDER 4: GO TO 10

The above will remain in the
loop until the user presses
BREAK. If you want to include a
test for a keypress you need to
keep it to a minimum. Try...

10 BORDER 6: BORDER 6: BORDER 3:
BORDER 4: IF NOT CODE INKEY$
THEN GO TO 10

           ...which will proceed
to the next line when a key is
pressed. Alternatively you could
use SUPA-QUIT from Issue 17.

If you want the routine to "time
out" after a set time try...

5 POKE 23673,7

10 PAUSE 1: BORDER 5: BORDER 5:
BORDER 5: BORDER 5: BORDER 1:
BORDER 4: GO TO PEEK 23673

Address 23673 is part of a
system variable that acts like a
clock and will increase by 1

about every 5 seconds. The GO TO
will first GO TO 7 and drop back
into line 10. After 5 seconds it
will GO TO 8 and so on until the
value in 23673 reaches 11 when
it will finally escape line 10
and proceed with the program.

Any IFs etc. in the line may
throw out the timing and the
whole thing collapses. I never
did manage to find a way in
"TICKET" to both detect a
keypress AND have a "time-out"
in the same line which is why
sometimes the program would not
proceed no matter how much you
bash the keyboard! Since then I
have written SUPA-QUIT which, I
feel sure, will now enable me to
do this.

To "synchronise" the BORDER
stripes with on-screen graphics
you need to plan a rough idea
first,e.g. say you want a simple
cyan sky for half the screen and
blue sea in the bottom half.Try:

10 BORDER 5: BORDER 5: etc..:
BORDER 1: GO TO etc. whatever is
needed in the program.

Run it and note where the stripe
reaches on screen. (I often use
FOR Y = 0 TO 21: PRINT Y: NEXT Y
to make this clear).Now you must
design your graphic - whether a
complex high-res screen created
in ARTIST II or just a plain
cyan-and blue screen - but with
the join MATCHING the join in
the BORDER.

NOTE WELL!The position of the
BORDER stripe will move as you
add more and more lines of BASIC
or even if you DIMension an
array and use up more memory so
you must finally calibrate it
when your program is completely
finished!

Fine adjustments can be made by
adding and removing SPACES
between the colon and the first
BORDER command but you need to
get it approximately right first
as there is a limit. In "TICKET"
I used variables: BORDER A:
BORDER B: etc. and it even made
a difference which variables
were declared first because of
the time it takes the system to
locate the variable!

I should also add that you must
put the routine near the start
of large programs as it takes a
fraction of a second longer for
the Spectrum to run higher line
numbers (and this routine cannot
spare a fraction of a second!).
Add another line:11 RETURN after
the routine then you can use GO
SUB to call it from anywhere.

You will also find there is a
maximum number of stripes you
can achieve and this will depend
on the size of the program.

Once the technique is mastered
you still need a lot of patience
but,like all creative endeavour,
the most important ingredient is
imagination!
                    - Brian

From: Ken Davies
Flat 8b,

Dear Brian & Co,

One of your readers was asking
about Artist 2 in Outlet No.15.
Well, there is a version for the
+3, but it has the old book for
Artist 2 128. It is about `19.00
and you get the sprite designer
and screen compressor. The page
maker is built in but if you
want to use a writer file you
have to load them in by tape. It
seems okay as I have not got any
artist programs for my +3.

I have all the Tasword programs
for the +3, Masterfile +3, also
the CP/M which, for anybody
interested, is quiet complex and
anybody getting it should be
prepared to spend a lot of time
and patience to find out how it
works. I have just joined The
Public Domain Library. They have
lots of software for CP/M.I also
have a few games on disk which
came with the machine.

Well at last I am using my Plus
Three with Interface 1 and
microdrives. I would like to
thank Brian Gaff for his help.
He is doing a little board and
cable that fits into the Plus
Three expansion port with a
small ribbon cable and it costs

`10 from him or if you are any
good at electronics he will send
you a diagram to do it yourself.

Well me being thick paid the
full price and it works okay as
I am writing this letter to you
using Tasword 2 and Interface 1
for the printer. You cannot use
the Plus Three BASIC with
Interface 1 connected you just
remove the Interface 1 from the
expansion port. Also you can use
the Multiface 128 but only in
48k mode with interface 1. Well
enough of that and onto some
other subject...

I went to the Northern Sinclair
Show on Sat April 8th 1989. As I
only live 25 miles from the


venue. Well, what did I think of
it? Well my own personal view
was good as I have not been to
one of those shows down in
London as it was too far to go.
For the first show it was not
bad but I think that with a bit
more thought it could have been
better but we should not
complain about that as it was
the first show.

Well I spent about `40 there.
There was more for the old Q.L.
than the Spectrum. There was
loads of software and there were
loads of microdrive cartridges
being sold but a lot of the
cartridges were used ones and
were ex Q.L. cartridges. You can
still use these on the Spectrum

if you reformat them to the
Spectrum. I have had 10 and
formatted them and they work
alright. They were selling these
at a `1 each. They also had
commas interfaces and software
for all Spectrums and they
looked very good. Pity I have
not got a phone. They had the
usual offers of printers and
discs at special prices and disc
boxes and printer stands. Also
different types of stationery
which included sheets of paper
and address labels of 1 or 2 or
3 across. Also new and
reconditioned microdrives at
very reasonable prices but the
old Interface 1 was not much on
show. I only saw about 3 and
they were going for about `35

which was dear. Re-conditioned
microdrives were going for about
`12-14 and new ones for about
`23-30 which is not too bad.
There were a few computer clubs
but if anyone had a Q.L. there
were lots of things and software
with disc drives for the machine
and I thought it well represent-
ed. Who said the Q.L. was dead?
Keep going you Q.L. All machines
require this support. You can
print my address if anybody
wants to write to me.
               -  Ken Davies
Thanks for the info, Ken. I'm
amazed at how many readers have
art programs yet we rarely get a
screen sent in or a program with
any graphics! (one exception was
COMMANDER in Issue 20) - Brian

Dear Each,

Thank you very much for my
latest issue of OUTLET(No.20).
Excellence upon yet more Excel-
lence. What paper based Mag.
could produce a front cover
picture to rival yours. None of
course and never can they. Mind

have noticed that none of your

ers are of the 'fair' sex.I know
of course,that the computer

users of this world are not

great plan, which for whatever

birthday celebrations in the


same amount of standard time. On

               - Hugh Mcgregor

by coincidence, a SHOUTBURST is

From Patrick Kirkham,  TENBY

Dear Ron,



This print out is from Tasword 2



on my HR5 printer. I can't close



the gaps between lines!Any help?



        Yours sincerely,

              Patrick

To Patrick Kirkham from Brian

The same principle applies here
as with previous letters - the
more info you send in about any
problem, the more chance of a
quick solution.

Firstly, in Tasword 2, when you
select P to Print you should see
the prompt: "Line Spacing? (1)".
Does the figure 1 appear on your
screen and do you just press
ENTER or do you enter 2? Do you
set the print-out margins?If so,
try again without setting them.
They may be forcing an extra
line feed. Check your printer
manual to see if the dipswitches
are set correctly. There should
be one titled something like:

                       ON    OFF
CR (AUTO FEED XT)  LF after
                    Print

Try setting that to OFF if it is
set to ON.


I have no information as to what
printer interface you are using.
If it requiries initialization
such us OPEN #3;"B"for Interface
1 or COPY : REM CHR$ 0 for the
Kempston where have you put
these lines in Tasword's BASIC?
Try entering BASIC in Tasword
and EDIT line 6000 (or whichever
line you used if different) and
add at the start of the line(but
after OPEN# 3 "B"if you're using
Interface 1)...

6000 LPRINT CHR$ 27;"A";CHR$ 2

Experiment with different values
instead of the 2 if it doesn't
quite work. Alternatively,define
a graphic (refer to the Tasword
2 manual) as 27, 65, 2 and put
the graphic at the top of the
next page you type into Tasword.

Let me know how you get on and
send any other details which may
help.
                       - Brian

From: Malcolm Phillips, Swansea.

Dear Ron/Brian,
Some time ago I used the lines
listed below in a game which
linked numbered guesses input
from the keyboard to letters in
a string.Numbers 1-50 related to
25 pairs of letters (see below).
The essence of the game was j$
would be "jumbled" differently
each time the program was RUN.

 550 LET a$="aabbccddeeffgghhiij
jkkllmmnnooppqqrrssttuuvvwwxxyy"
2600 LET j$=""
2650 FOR k=1 to 50
2700 LET l=LEN a$
2750 LET n=INT   (RND*l)+1
2800 LET j$=j$+a$(n)
2850 LET a$=a$(TO n-1)+a$(n+1 TO
): NEXT k

This was the "jumble" routine.

The program worked fine and it
was further enhanced when I used
CHUNKY from issue 5(doesn't time
fly?).

All was well until I noticed
something strange...

Each time the program was RUN it
would act exactly as the time
before. Somehow line 2750 put
the same values in the same
order into variable n so that
the game was predictable! Every
time I ran the program all the
guesses gave the same results!

This, of course, spoiled the
game but created a problem that

was/is beyond me. Can you help
or explain what is going on? By
the way, if the GOSUB 9995 isn't
called then the program acts as
it was intended to, i.e. var n
generates a random number each
time and therefore a differently
jumbled j$.

               Mystified, Mal.

P.S. If you add a line to the
above which PRINTs out var n
before using/calling CHUNKY and
then after you will see what I
mean. As it is it limits the use
of CHUNKY (to the point that I
can't even use it!

P.P.S. It's driving me MAD!

To Malcolm Phillips from Brian

Dear Mystified Mal,

Your query gives detailed info
about the problem enabling me to
solve it immediately!

Whenever you use the function
RND it takes the value from a
system variable called SEED at
addresses 23670 and 23671 from
which the next random value is
calculated. A new value is then
put in SEED for the next RND. If
you use the command RANDOMIZE
followed by a number this will
set the value in SEED to that
number. If this is done before
using RND then RND will always
produce the same random number
sequence.

If you look at the CHUNKY REM at
line 9995 you will see I used a
RANDOMIZE statement with a USR
to set up the CHUNKY characters.
This will place the same value
in SEED every time you start
your program!So you're not going
mad after all! One can use LET X
= USR or PRINT USR instead (but
don't EDIT line 9995 or I think
it will crash!). However, using
a variable in a general-purpose
routine may cause problems if
the programmer uses it elsewhere
and calls the routine without
realizing it and PRINT USR will
PRINT a number on the screen! I
suppose I could use a weird
variable name in future GO SUB
REM routines like LET REMSTORE =
USR etc..

The solution is to put RANDOMIZE
without a number (or with the
number 0 which does the same) in
a line AFTER you GO SUB 9995.
This will put a random value in
SEED and all should be well. In
practice I sometimes think it
necessary to put two or three
RANDOMIZE commands in a row to
really jumble it up as over the
years I've found some situations
where I still seem to get
similar values e.g. a string of
low values all the time. I've
never been able to pin this down
exactly but would be interested
if anyone else has noticed this
or if I'm going crazy!

Incidentally, you can use
RANDOMIZE followed by a value to


DELIBERATELY create the same
sequence of values from RND.This
can be very useful, particularly
when testing a program or I have
used it to force a preferred
graphic display from a "random"
routine.
                        -Brian

To Alistair Thomas from Brian

To take your last question first I must say it's a fascinating idea and I think it would work! I have added this to my project list and will see what I can do. If it works out I'll put it in a future issue. Meanwhile you may care to read AUTOINFO in Issue 7 which describes exactly how AUTOCHARS works in great detail and also OUTCLASS in Issue 5 for tips on saving memory.

Now, the border graphics effect is created thus:

10 PAUSE 1 : BORDER 6 : BORDER 4 : BORDER 5 : BORDER 0: BORDER 2: BORDER 7 : GO TO 10

I think it works because the PAUSE 1 delays the video signal by one fiftieth of a second which exactly matches the time it takes for the BORDER command to fully change. You can also experiment with the PAUSE 1 at the end of the BORDER commands rather than at the front. To get thicker stripes you just repeat, e.g.

10 PAUSE 1: BORDER 5: BORDER 5: BORDER 5: BORDER 5: BORDER 5: BORDER 4: GO TO 10

The above will remain in the loop until the user presses BREAK. If you want to include a test for a keypress you need to keep it to a minimum. Try...

10 BORDER 6: BORDER 6: BORDER 3: BORDER 4: IF NOT CODE INKEY$ THEN GO TO 10

...which will proceed to the next line when a key is pressed. Alternatively you could use SUPA-QUIT from Issue 17.

If you want the routine to "time out" after a set time try...

5 POKE 23673,7

10 PAUSE 1: BORDER 5: BORDER 5: BORDER 5: BORDER 5: BORDER 1: BORDER 4: GO TO PEEK 23673

Address 23673 is part of a system variable that acts like a clock and will increase by 1

about every 5 seconds. The GO TO will first GO TO 7 and drop back into line 10. After 5 seconds it will GO TO 8 and so on until the value in 23673 reaches 11 when it will finally escape line 10 and proceed with the program.

Any IFs etc. in the line may throw out the timing and the whole thing collapses. I never did manage to find a way in "TICKET" to both detect a keypress AND have a "time-out" in the same line which is why sometimes the program would not proceed no matter how much you bash the keyboard! Since then I have written SUPA-QUIT which, I feel sure, will now enable me to do this.

To "synchronise" the BORDER stripes with on-screen graphics you need to plan a rough idea first,e.g. say you want a simple cyan sky for half the screen and blue sea in the bottom half.Try:

10 BORDER 5: BORDER 5: etc..: BORDER 1: GO TO etc. whatever is needed in the program.

Run it and note where the stripe reaches on screen. (I often use FOR Y = 0 TO 21: PRINT Y: NEXT Y to make this clear).Now you must design your graphic - whether a complex high-res screen created in ARTIST II or just a plain cyan-and blue screen - but with the join MATCHING the join in the BORDER.

NOTE WELL!The position of the BORDER stripe will move as you add more and more lines of BASIC or even if you DIMension an array and use up more memory so you must finally calibrate it when your program is completely finished!

Fine adjustments can be made by adding and removing SPACES between the colon and the first BORDER command but you need to get it approximately right first as there is a limit. In "TICKET" I used variables: BORDER A: BORDER B: etc. and it even made a difference which variables were declared first because of the time it takes the system to locate the variable!

I should also add that you must put the routine near the start of large programs as it takes a fraction of a second longer for the Spectrum to run higher line numbers (and this routine cannot spare a fraction of a second!). Add another line:11 RETURN after the routine then you can use GO SUB to call it from anywhere.

You will also find there is a maximum number of stripes you can achieve and this will depend on the size of the program.

Once the technique is mastered you still need a lot of patience but,like all creative endeavour, the most important ingredient is imagination! - Brian

Dear Ron/Brian, Some time ago I used the lines listed below in a game which linked numbered guesses input from the keyboard to letters in a string.Numbers 1-50 related to 25 pairs of letters (see below). The essence of the game was j$ would be "jumbled" differently each time the program was RUN.

This was the "jumble" routine.

The program worked fine and it was further enhanced when I used CHUNKY from issue 5(doesn't time fly?).

All was well until I noticed something strange...

Each time the program was RUN it would act exactly as the time before. Somehow line 2750 put the same values in the same order into variable n so that the game was predictable! Every time I ran the program all the guesses gave the same results!

This, of course, spoiled the game but created a problem that

was/is beyond me. Can you help or explain what is going on? By the way, if the GOSUB 9995 isn't called then the program acts as it was intended to, i.e. var n generates a random number each time and therefore a differently jumbled j$.

Mystified, Mal.

P.S. If you add a line to the above which PRINTs out var n before using/calling CHUNKY and then after you will see what I mean. As it is it limits the use of CHUNKY (to the point that I can't even use it!

P.P.S. It's driving me MAD!

To Malcolm Phillips from Brian

Dear Mystified Mal,

Your query gives detailed info about the problem enabling me to solve it immediately!

Whenever you use the function RND it takes the value from a system variable called SEED at addresses 23670 and 23671 from which the next random value is calculated. A new value is then put in SEED for the next RND. If you use the command RANDOMIZE followed by a number this will set the value in SEED to that number. If this is done before using RND then RND will always produce the same random number sequence.

If you look at the CHUNKY REM at line 9995 you will see I used a RANDOMIZE statement with a USR to set up the CHUNKY characters. This will place the same value in SEED every time you start your program!So you're not going mad after all! One can use LET X = USR or PRINT USR instead (but don't EDIT line 9995 or I think it will crash!). However, using a variable in a general-purpose routine may cause problems if the programmer uses it elsewhere and calls the routine without realizing it and PRINT USR will PRINT a number on the screen! I suppose I could use a weird variable name in future GO SUB REM routines like LET REMSTORE = USR etc..

The solution is to put RANDOMIZE without a number (or with the number 0 which does the same) in a line AFTER you GO SUB 9995. This will put a random value in SEED and all should be well. In practice I sometimes think it necessary to put two or three RANDOMIZE commands in a row to really jumble it up as over the years I've found some situations where I still seem to get similar values e.g. a string of low values all the time. I've never been able to pin this down exactly but would be interested if anyone else has noticed this or if I'm going crazy!

Incidentally, you can use RANDOMIZE followed by a value to

DELIBERATELY create the same sequence of values from RND.This can be very useful, particularly when testing a program or I have used it to force a preferred graphic display from a "random" routine.

Теперь о том, как создаётся графический эффект на бордюре:

```text
10 PAUSE 1 : BORDER 6 : BORDER 4 : BORDER 5 : BORDER 0: BORDER 2: BORDER 7 : GO TO 10
```

Думаю, это работает потому, что `PAUSE 1` задерживает видеосигнал на одну пятидесятую секунды, что точно соответствует времени, необходимому для полной смены команды `BORDER`. Вы также можете поэкспериментировать, поставив `PAUSE 1` в конец команд `BORDER`, а не в начало. Чтобы получить полосы толще, просто повторите команду, например:

```text
10 PAUSE 1: BORDER 5: BORDER 5: BORDER 5: BORDER 5: BORDER 5: BORDER 4: GO TO 10
```

Этот код будет крутиться в цикле до тех пор, пока пользователь не нажмёт BREAK. Если вы хотите добавить проверку нажатия клавиши, её нужно свести к минимуму. Попробуйте...

```text
10 BORDER 6: BORDER 6: BORDER 3: BORDER 4: IF NOT CODE INKEY$ THEN GO TO 10
```

...и программа перейдёт к следующей строке при нажатии любой клавиши. Либо вы можете использовать SUPA-QUIT из выпуска 17.

Если вы хотите, чтобы подпрограмма завершалась по тайм-ауту через заданное время, попробуйте:

```text
5 POKE 23673,7
10 PAUSE 1: BORDER 5: BORDER 5: BORDER 5: BORDER 5: BORDER 1: BORDER 4: GO TO PEEK 23673
```

Адрес 23673 — это часть системной переменной, работающей как таймер: её значение увеличивается на 1 примерно каждые 5 секунд. Команда `GO TO` сначала перейдёт на строку 7 и тут же провалится обратно в строку 10. Через 5 секунд произойдёт переход на строку 8 и так далее, пока значение в 23673 не достигнет 11 — тогда выполнение наконец вырвется из строки 10 и пойдёт дальше по программе.

Любые `IF` и прочие конструкции в этой строке могут сбить тайминги, и весь эффект развалится. Мне так и не удалось в игре «TICKET» найти способ одновременно опрашивать клавиатуру И задавать тайм-аут в одной и той же строке, из-за чего программа иногда отказывалась продолжать работу, как бы вы ни колотили по клавишам! С тех пор я написал процедуру SUPA-QUIT, которая, как мне кажется, теперь позволит мне это сделать.

Чтобы «синхронизировать» полосы на бордюре с экранной графикой, сначала нужно всё приблизительно спланировать. Скажем, вы хотите простое голубое небо на верхней половине экрана и синее море на нижней. Попробуйте:

```text
10 BORDER 5: BORDER 5: etc..: BORDER 1: GO TO etc.
```
— или что там потребуется по программе.

Запустите и заметьте, на каком уровне полоса стыкуется с экраном. (Я часто использую `FOR Y = 0 TO 21: PRINT Y: NEXT Y`, чтобы это было нагляднее). Теперь вы должны нарисовать свою графику — будь то сложная high-res картинка, созданная в ARTIST II, или просто заливка голубым и синим — но так, чтобы линия раздела СОВПАДАЛА с линией раздела на BORDER.

ОБРАТИТЕ ВНИМАНИЕ! Позиция полосы бордюра будет смещаться по мере добавления новых строк Бейсика или даже если вы зададите массив через `DIM` и займёте больше памяти, так что окончательную калибровку нужно делать тогда, когда программа уже полностью готова!

Тонкую подстройку можно выполнять добавлением и удалением пробелов между двоеточием и первой командой `BORDER`, но сначала нужно попасть примерно в цель, так как диапазон регулировки ограничен. В «TICKET» я использовал переменные: `BORDER A`: `BORDER B`: и т. д., и даже имело значение, какие переменные были объявлены первыми — из-за времени, которое требуется системе на их поиск!

Я также должен добавить, что эту процедуру нужно размещать ближе к началу больших программ, поскольку у Спектрума уходит на долю секунды больше времени на переход к строкам с большими номерами (а эта процедура не может позволить себе потерять даже долю секунды!). Добавьте ещё одну строку: `11 RETURN` после процедуры, и тогда вы сможете вызывать её через `GO SUB` откуда угодно.

Вы также заметите, что существует предельное количество полос, которого можно добиться, и оно зависит от размера программы.

Как только техника будет освоена, вам всё равно понадобится много терпения, но, как и в любом творческом начинании, самый главный ингредиент — это воображение!

**Малкольму Филлипсу от Брайана:**

Дорогой озадаченный Mal,

Ваш вопрос содержит подробную информацию о проблеме, что позволило мне решить ее немедленно!

Всякий раз, когда вы используете функцию `RND`, она берет значение из системной переменной с именем SEED по адресам 23670 и 23671, на основе которой вычисляется следующее случайное значение. Затем в SEED записывается новое значение для следующего `RND`. Если использовать команду `RANDOMIZE`, за которой следует число, это установит значение в SEED равным этому числу. Если сделать это перед использованием `RND`, то `RND` всегда будет выдавать одну и ту же последовательность случайных чисел.

Если вы посмотрите на REM-строку процедуры CHUNKY в строке 9995, то увидите, что я использовал оператор `RANDOMIZE` с `USR` для настройки символов CHUNKY. Это помещает одно и то же значение в SEED при каждом запуске вашей программы! Так что вы вовсе не сходите с ума! Вместо этого можно использовать `LET X = USR` или `PRINT USR` (но не редактируйте строку 9995, иначе, полагаю, она сбросится!). Однако использование переменной в универсальной подпрограмме может вызвать проблемы, если программист использует ее в другом месте и вызовет процедуру, не подозревая об этом, а `PRINT USR` выведет число на экран! Полагаю, в будущем в таких процедурах вызова через GO SUB REM я мог бы использовать какое-нибудь странное имя переменной вроде `LET REMSTORE = USR` и т.д.

Решение состоит в том, чтобы поместить команду `RANDOMIZE` без числа (или с числом 0, что дает тот же эффект) в строке ПОСЛЕ вызова `GO SUB 9995`. Это запишет случайное значение в SEED, и все наладится. На практике я иногда считаю необходимым ставить две или три команды `RANDOMIZE` подряд, чтобы как следует всё перемешать, поскольку с годами я сталкивался с ситуациями, когда все еще продолжали выпадать схожие значения — например, цепочка малых чисел подряд. Мне так и не удалось выяснить точную причину, но мне было бы интересно узнать, замечал ли это кто-то еще, или это я схожу с ума!

К слову, вы можете использовать `RANDOMIZE`, за которым следует значение, чтобы

НАМЕРЕННО создавать одну и ту же последовательность значений из RND. Это может быть очень полезно, особенно при тестировании программы, либо я использовал это, чтобы принудительно получить желаемое графическое изображение из «случайной» подпрограммы.  
— Brian
